utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, before I let you continue, it would be good if you would not read into the transcript the content of the note before we decide whether you can use it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. If I could just simply put it this way: I would like to ask the witness if he recalls telling the Croatian police, the day after the incident when the note was made, whether he, at that time, indicated that he had seen Mr. Hadzic. The witness's recollection on this issue was not in dispute until the cross-examination. It's not something -- back where I come from we would say bolstering. I don't know that it would have been appropriate to bolster the evidence during the direct by asking, inviting the witness, to talk about having talked to this -- talked to the Croatian authorities about it the following day. He simply saw what he saw. What's relevant now that his recollection -- the identification's been challenged is, in our view, the fact that on the very next day he identified Hadzic to local authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stringer, please tell me if I'm missing something. This isn't a situation where we're dealing with a witness's account of events and where, because of the passage of time, it is of assistance in terms of his initial report. What is under challenge here is a much narrower question. It is the issue of the quality of his identification at the time. So does it matter what his report was the following today as contrasts all the way up to when he gave evidence this morning? Because that is what the challenge is. So how would we be assisted by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We see that it's relevant because the video that was shown of the man walking out of the building that was shown repeatedly -- I mean, the witness has indicated he can't say or he doesn't remember. He doesn't remember. And to the extent that the witness has now indicated he doesn't remember, it may not be the dispositive fact. Obviously it's all before the Trial Chamber. But if, in fact, the witness said the very following day to an official that he identified or he saw Goran Hadzic on this location, we think it is a relevant piece of evidence that is a part of -- that ought to be part of the Chamber's consideration, given that the events we're talking about here occurred about 21 years ago or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Anything from you, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. To the extent that it's relevant in terms of what was said during the chief, the witness actually didn't refer to the note in question. What the witness said was that he brought the ID and the person -- so he hands the ID over and he says: "The person I talked to made an unofficial note of it. I handed it over." There's no indication that this witness actually knows or at the time knew of the creation of this Official Note, which is an entirely different thing. It's an account of, allegedly, what he saw. That's not what he referred to in direct examination. So to the extent that that's relevant to Your Honours, that part of the record needs to be corrected. Secondly, the Prosecutor said that he felt constrained not to raise this document on chief because it would be improper bolstering. Well, if it's improper bolstering on chief, it's improper bolstering -- far more improper on re-direct. That's the second point. And the third point is that I couldn't agree more with Judge Hall's remark that the challenge was in respect of the witness's identification. Nothing in the intervening years makes any difference to that, and so, therefore, this document is not relevant. Unless, Your Honours, a whole bunch of relevant material from the document starts coming in, and then you'll find that the entire line of examination was conducted very deliberately to avoid it, and the cross was conducted in a way to -- in a manner that reflected their avoidance of those issues. And now that the cross has been conducted, the horse is out of the barn, and the Prosecutor's trying to get a second bite of the apple. It's as simple as, that, and it's not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There will be no -- let me double-check before I say. There's no further re-direct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll have the witness brought back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could make one remark after the witness has completed his testimony, and perhaps if there's time raise one other issue that's unrelated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I've been instructed the ruling is that we cannot ask the witness if he referred to having seen Hadzic on the following day when he spoke to the Croatian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that's the ruling, I would like to ask the question without referring to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pinter, earlier we were talking about the occasion when you turned over that identification to the Croatian authorities in Osijek. Do you recall when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PINTER
utterances.text: It was on the following day or the day after I returned from Dalj. I think it was on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at that time, do you recall if you mentioned to them that you had seen Mr. Hadzic at the Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I am going to object on the same grounds as previously. I know Your Honour has just indicated that the ruling was that he can't use the note. You didn't say whether or not you would allow him to go further. So now I am interposing an objection to the question itself for the same reasons that have previously been mentioned. Whether the note is used or not is somewhat neither here nor there. It's going into the issue that could have been gone into during the direct examination, and they chose not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution would have known about your position on this issue, Mr. Gosnell, objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pinter, do you want me to ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time you met with the Croatian authorities, do you recall if you mentioned to them that you had seen Mr. Hadzic at the Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pinter, this is the end of your testimony. You're now released as a witness. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist us. The court usher will escort you out of court, and we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Prosecution submits that the record should reflect that the Defence did not put to the witness the proposition that he was mistaken in his identification and that Hadzic was not present. That's how we interpret the cross-examination. The issue might surface in the future. It might be useful. I don't know if the Chamber or if the Defence even shares the Prosecution view on this, but in our view, it was not put to the witness certainly in the way that, in our respectful submission, ought to be done. And it perhaps would be useful to know whether that view is shared because I'm not -- we will not raise objections of -- along these lines if, in fact, the Chamber views that we got close enough to it today that it was put to the witness. I just mention that, that in our view it was not put to the witness, and the issue has not been perfected, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the line of questions that was put, can there be any possible other interpretation but that it was a challenge to the witness's initial assertion that he saw the accused when he went to Dalj?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Certainly that interpretation can be drawn, Your Honour. My experience in this institution is that different Judges coming from different backgrounds could possibly differ on whether, despite whatever interpretation can be drawn, the express rule of the language has been met, and that's why I raise it as a way of asking for the Chamber's guidance. I can tell Your Honour I've been called out by a Judge from a different country for not having put it more directly on a very similar issue. And so it's something I think that possibly Judges can disagree on. And being an American, it's not an issue that I've dealt with tremendously in my pre-Tribunal experience, I should add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just a brief remark -- well, two remarks. Specifically, I do believe that the issue was put squarely and fairly to the witness, challenging whether or not he had -- could identify this person as Mr. Hadzic. I think his testimony was clear on that. And I don't think that Rule 90(H) is a technical rule involving perfection of questions. I believe what Rule 90(H) is about is to prevent either party from holding back an issue with a highly relevant witness and not asking questions about it and then, at the end of the case, putting together evidence in a certain sequence to present a certain proposition that is directly contrary to what a highly relevant witness would have been able to comment upon. I believe that's the purpose of Rule 90(H), not, you know, whether or not you call the witness a liar or say: Did you completely -- you know, isn't it true that you can't say that that's Mr. Hadzic after a line of ten questions, in which he said: I can't identify. So I don't believe it's a technical rule. I believe it has a broader purpose. And when you look at the way in which Rule 90(H) has been interpreted in Judgements, it certainly hasn't been given that technical interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Gosnell, did you put to the witness your position that Mr. Hadzic was not present at that moment and at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And does that make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe that once you've received certain answers from a witness in which he indicates that he cannot say for certain who it was, then the additional question, I would say, is redundant. Especially -- especially, Your Honours, when it was on the record what our position is. It's not really so much the witness being -- answering an obvious question in an obvious way when you've already got the predicate answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you have another question, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is unrelated. For future practice -- and this relates generally to the conduct of the trial and the public's right to -- or the public nature of the trial. Because, of course, the trial is being followed, and that's a good thing, in our view. The Prosecution -- our 92 ter witnesses, it's our understanding that when a 92 ter witness testifies and a 92 ter statement is admitted even as a public document, it's not readily available to the public. And so the essence of the witness testimony is not readily, therefore, available to the public because, of course, as a 92 ter witness, we simply cut to specific issues or clarifications. In its pre-trial guide-lines, the Chamber indicated that it -- that the Prosecution need not read a summary of the witness's testimony before beginning, and that's been done in other cases. It's not been required here, and we've not been doing it. But the end result is that for the public who wish to follow the proceedings, it's -- can be difficult for them to really have an idea of what the witness evidence is about, at least on the direct examination, because the bulk of it is in the statement itself. And the Prosecution would like to -- we were -- are considering changing the practice to provide some very brief summary or overview of the witness's evidence. We would prefer to do it, however, outside the presence of the witness, because it's probably something that's better done without the witness listening to the Prosecution purporting to summarise their evidence. So there's some tension there. But we think that there's a public trial issue. There is an access issue, if I can put it that way, that needs to be addressed, and it's certainly not something to be decided today or, you know, urgently. But I just wanted to mention it to the Chamber, and it's perhaps a conversation that -- communications can continue among the parties and the Chamber in the coming weeks because we would -- the Prosecution would like to have -- find a way to address this so that more information can be available to those who wish to follow the case, particularly in respect of these 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Does the Defence have an instant view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The initial view is that summaries are not particularly helpful. They are, of course, one party's interpretation of the statement, usually not entirely shared in all regards by the other party. And we believe that the agencies that cover this Tribunal do an excellent job of reviewing witness testimony and making it available to such news sources as are interested to pick them up. SENSE agency does an excellent job of reviewing and summarising testimony. So we would say there's no particular reason to make such summaries available for the purposes of publicity, and given that they're often somewhat biased and slanted, it's not particularly helpful to the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to mention that, in fact, SENSE is one of the parties - there have been several - who've expressed frustration, if I can put it that way, with the issue. And so that's among a number of reasons why I've raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the issue and come back to you later, as soon as possible. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to say with trepidation that the Prosecution does not have any additional witnesses for today, Mr. President. Again, I regret the down time that we've had this week and we're working to prevent that in the future, but it does happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything from the Defence? Court adjourned.
